title: 5 Enterprise AI Agent Use Cases That Work: StackAI's Bernard Aceituno for Forbes
summary: Which AI agent use cases actually work in regulated industries? StackAI cofounder Bernard Aceituno shares five proven examples. Featured in Forbes.
body_text: Bernard Aceituno, cofounder of StackAI, was featured in Forbes to answer a question circulating in the enterprise AI world: which agent use cases are actually working inside regulated organizations right now? Drawing on three years embedded in enterprise AI deployments across financial services, legal, healthcare, and more, Aceituno observes that the highest-value agents tend to share three traits: they're event-triggered, they translate a real-world process directly into software, and they integrate tightly with the systems where work already lives. He organizes five proven use cases by industry. In private capital, a triggered workflow handles the top of the funnel: an inbound deal email is classified by sector and stage, attachments are parsed, a financial summary is extracted and screened against the firm's criteria, and a preliminary memo is drafted into the CRM, so associates open their morning queue to find the initial work already done. For law firms and legal teams, a contract landing in a shared folder moves through agents that extract key clauses, compare them against the firm's playbook and precedent, and draft a redline summary routed to a reviewing attorney, ensuring nothing is sent without approval. In healthcare, a human-in-the-loop system for prior authorization assembles clinical evidence from the EHR, retrieves payer criteria, drafts the authorization letter, and routes it to a nurse case manager who approves, edits, or rejects in seconds. In insurance, a triggered workflow integrated with the policy admin system classifies each broker submission, parses attachments, extracts and validates structured risk data, and drafts an acknowledgment, replacing the first hour of manual data entry. In banking, an agentic workflow built for internal audit reads a program, determines which fields to check, and runs specialist sub-agents that extract facts and place tick marks on source documents, turning hours of per-file review into a first cut in minutes with far broader coverage. Aceituno closes with three takeaways: nearly all high-value agents are triggered rather than chat-based, each use case blends deterministic actions with LLM reasoning and human-in-the-loop steps for business-critical moments, and integrations matter because the most useful agents can reach every system needed to close the loop. His advice to CIOs is to ignore the noise and study the patterns that work in reality. Read the full article here .

body_text: TL;DR Vibecodeapp was blocked from the App Store in March 2026 under Apple’s Guideline 2.5.2 crackdown. If you’re looking for Vibecodeapp alternatives, your best options depend on what you need: x1 for native Swift iOS apps that pass App Review, Rork or Newly for cross-platform React Native builds, Superapp for budget-friendly native iOS development, FlutterFlow for teams wanting a visual builder, and Cursor or Claude Code for technical founders who prefer writing their own code. Why This List Exists In March 2026, Apple pulled Vibecodeapp from the App Store. It wasn’t alone. Replit and another vibe coding app called “Anything” were also blocked the same month, all cited for violating Guideline 2.5.2, the rule requiring apps to be “self-contained” without downloading or executing code that introduces new features. The timing was predictable. App Store submissions surged 84% year-over-year in Q1 2026, with 235,800 new apps hitting review. Apple’s system, designed for a world of professional developers submitting apps one at a time, buckled under the volume of AI-generated submissions. The crackdown was the response. This matters because the vibe coding tools market has reached an estimated $4.7 billion in 2026, growing at 38% annually. People who never would have built an app before are now building them. But the tool you choose determines whether your app survives App Review or gets killed before it launches. The search for Vibecodeapp alternatives is really a search for something more specific: which tools produce standalone native apps you compile and submit yourself (safe from Apple’s enforcement) versus which tools act as an “app within an app” on your phone (exactly what Apple targeted)? This guide answers that question for every major option on the market. See how x1 compares to Vibecodeapp in a head-to-head breakdown. At-a-Glance Comparison Table Tool Starting Price Output Type True iOS Native? Android? Code Export Free Tier Best For x1 $99/mo ($66 yearly) Native Swift/Xcode Yes No Full Xcode project ~100 credits Serious iOS founders Rork $25/mo React Native/Expo (Swift via Max) Via Expo or Max tier Yes GitHub export 35 credits/mo Cross-platform MVPs Superapp $25/mo Native Swift/SwiftUI Yes No Yes 5 daily credits Budget iOS builders Newly $25/mo React Native/Expo Via Expo Yes Full code Limited free Code ownership focus FlutterFlow ~$80/mo/seat Flutter (Dart) Compiled native Yes Flutter code Free to build Teams with visual builder Cursor ~$20/mo Whatever you code Depends on you Depends on you Your code Free tier Technical builders Claude Code API usage Whatever you code Depends on you Depends on you Your code Pay-per-token Experienced devs Vibra Code Free (self-host) React Native/Expo Via Expo Yes Open source Fully free OSS enthusiasts Why People Are Switching From Vibecodeapp Before getting into alternatives, it helps to understand the specific pain points driving this search. They go beyond the Apple ban. The Apple removal. Vibecodeapp was directly blocked from App Store updates in March 2026. For anyone building an iOS app, this creates an obvious trust problem. If the tool itself can’t stay on the platform, how confident can you be in apps it generates? No Android support. Vibecodeapp outputs apps for Apple platforms only. Cross-platform founders are stuck from the start. Source code behind a paywall. Trustpilot reviewers specifically call this out. One wrote: “in order to download your own source code you need to pay £50 / month.” For a tool marketed at beginners, locking code export behind a premium tier feels adversarial. Credit burn. This is the universal complaint across every AI app builder, not just Vibecodeapp. Users of Lovable, Bolt, Replit, Rork, and Vibecodeapp independently report spending roughly half their credits repairing bugs rather than building new features. The practical advice from practitioners: budget for about double the headline price. Understanding how AI app builder credits work before committing to any tool saves real money. Support quality. Vibecodeapp has only 4 Trustpilot reviews, and they’re overwhelmingly negative. One reviewer described filing an Apple Card chargeback and FTC fraud complaint, noting the support page didn’t even load. Another called the platform “broken” and recommended “anything but Vibecode.” These aren’t edge cases. They represent the core reasons people search for Vibecodeapp alternatives. The “Native” Question You Need to Understand First Not all Vibecodeapp alternatives produce the same kind of output, and the differences matter enormously for App Store approval and long-term app quality. There are three categories: True native Swift/SwiftUI. The tool generates actual Swift code and an Xcode project. This is what Apple expects. Apps built this way are indistinguishable from hand-coded apps during review. x1 and Superapp fall into this category. React Native/Expo compiled to native. The tool generates JavaScript-based React Native code that compiles into a native binary through Expo. Apple accepts these apps, and many successful App Store apps use React Native. Rork, Newly, and Vibecodeapp itself use this approach. Web wrappers. The tool generates a web app and wraps it in a native shell. Apple increasingly rejects these, and they perform noticeably worse. None of the alternatives on this list use this approach, but cheaper tools on the market often do. This distinction is worth understanding before comparing any tools. For a broader look at how these builder types differ , there’s a deeper breakdown available. 1. x1 Best for: Solo founders serious about shipping a polished native iOS app to the App Store x1 is a YC-backed (F24 batch) AI app studio that turns a plain-English description into a real, native iPhone app ready for the App Store. The output is native Swift and Xcode projects, not React Native, not web wrappers. What separates x1 from most Vibecodeapp alternatives is the structured workflow. Instead of a single prompt window where you describe everything at once (the “one-shot generation” approach that tends to produce fragile apps ), x1 breaks the process into five stages called studios: Plan — Map out screens, features, and app flow from sign-up through the main experience Design — Shape branding, layouts, buttons, spacing, and copy before code is generated Build — Generate the actual iPhone app screen by screen, with testing and fixes included Launch — Create App Store screenshots, write the listing, and submit for review, all in one place Iterate — Refine and polish after the initial build Pricing: Builder: $99/mo ($66/mo billed yearly) Pro: $199/mo ($133/mo billed yearly) Max: $299/mo ($200/mo billed yearly) Around 100 free credits to try before committing Try x1 with free credits to build out a feature before paying. Key strengths: Native Swift/Xcode output that’s unaffected by Apple’s Guideline 2.5.2 enforcement Built-in App Store screenshots, ASO metadata, and submission flow (most competitors stop at code generation) Ownership-first: you get a real Xcode project you can extend, modify, or hand to a developer Sequenced workflow reduces the credit burn problem by catching issues at each stage rather than at the end Tradeoffs: iOS only. No Android output. No free tier, just trial credits. The $99/mo entry point is higher than cross-platform alternatives. Early-stage product from a small team, meaning fewer public integrations and case studies than mature tools. Why it matters post-crackdown: Because x1 generates standalone Xcode projects you compile and submit yourself, the output is treated like any hand-coded app during Apple’s review. There’s no “app within an app” architecture to trigger Guideline 2.5.2. For iOS-focused founders evaluating Vibecodeapp alternatives, this is the cleanest answer to the Apple compliance question. For a detailed walkthrough of the full process, see how x1 works from idea to App Store readiness. 2. Rork Best for: Cross-platform MVP validation when you need both iOS and Android quickly Rork is an AI-powered mobile app builder that turns plain-English prompts into functional iOS and Android apps using React Native. Backed by $2.8 million from a16z, it’s attracted over 743,000 monthly visits and built real traction among non-technical founders and product managers. Pricing: Free tier with 35 credits/month Junior: $25/mo (100 AI messages) Senior: $100/mo (the sweet spot for building and iterating a full MVP) Enterprise: $200/mo Rork Max tier compiles native Swift apps that run across iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, Apple TV, and Vision Pro Key strengths: Cross-platform output from a single prompt Free tier lets you test before paying GitHub export for full code access Rork Max provides an upgrade path to native Swift if you outgrow React Native a16z backing suggests staying power Tradeoffs: No built-in database, authentication, payments, or push notifications without extra engineering help. For anything beyond a basic prototype, you’ll need additional tools or developer time. Free plan’s 5 daily credit limit is too restrictive for iterative building. Credit consumption for complex apps is unpredictable. The credit burn problem applies here too. Practitioners on Reddit report spending significant time fixing AI-introduced errors on Rork, same as other tools. For a deeper comparison of Rork and Vibecodeapp , there’s a detailed side-by-side available. Practitioner perspective: A highly-ranked Reddit thread in r/SideProject, where a user tested nearly all mobile vibe coding builders, notes that while Rork generates functional apps quickly, the quality differences between tools become apparent once you move past simple prototypes. 3. Superapp Best for: Budget-conscious iOS builders who want native Swift without owning a Mac Superapp generates native Swift and SwiftUI code, not web wrappers, not React Native. It runs in the browser and builds in the cloud, which means you don’t need a Mac to create an iOS app. For founders stuck on Windows or Linux, this alone makes it worth considering. A YouTube walkthrough of Superapp shows a user building a native iOS app and getting it to the App Store in about 25 minutes, providing visual proof that the workflow can move quickly for simple apps. Pricing: Free plan with 5 daily credits Pro: $25/mo Business: $50/mo Max: $100/mo Key strengths: Native Swift/SwiftUI output at the lowest price point for a true-native tool Browser-based, so no Mac required Supabase backend integration built in UI design follows Apple’s Human Interface Guidelines Tradeoffs: Credit-constrained, especially on lower tiers. Five daily credits on the free plan won’t get you far. Newer product with limited public reviews. Hard to judge reliability at scale. iOS only, same limitation as x1 but at a lower price with fewer workflow features. No built-in launch assets (screenshots, ASO metadata) that you’d get with more expensive tools. 4. Newly Best for: Cross-platform builders who want clean React Native code and full ownership Newly turns natural language prompts into functional iOS and Android apps using genuine React Native code on the Expo framework. The emphasis is on code quality and ownership. You get 100% source code access, and a one-click APK builder simplifies Android distribution. One notable feature for Vibecodeapp refugees: Windows users can build iOS apps without a Mac, similar to Superapp but with cross-platform output. Pricing: Starting at $25/mo Limited free tier available 10 minutes to first working app (their claim) Key strengths: Clean React Native/Expo codebase that developers report is readable and modifiable Cross-platform from a single prompt One-click APK builder for Android Full code ownership without paywall restrictions (unlike Vibecodeapp’s tiered export) Tradeoffs: Complex custom logic still needs manual refinement. The AI handles standard patterns well but struggles with unusual requirements. Monthly cost compounds over time, especially if you’re iterating heavily. Less established than FlutterFlow or Rork, with a smaller community for troubleshooting. 5. FlutterFlow Best for: Technical teams wanting a visual builder with exportable Flutter code FlutterFlow sits in a different category from the other Vibecodeapp alternatives on this list. It’s a visual, low-code platform for building native apps with Flutter, not a prompt-to-app AI tool. You drag and drop components, configure logic visually, and export real Flutter (Dart) code. This matters because FlutterFlow apps compile to native code for both iOS and Android. The exported source code is fully yours, which makes it a strong contender for teams worried about vendor lock-in. Pricing: ~$80/mo per seat Free tier to build (paid to export) Key strengths: Mature product with a large user community Full Flutter code export, no lock-in Cross-platform native compilation (iOS, Android, web, desktop) Visual approach suits designers and product managers More predictable than AI-first tools since you control every element directly Tradeoffs: Per-seat pricing gets expensive for teams. Two designers plus a developer means $240/mo before any other costs. Not AI-first. You’re building visually, not prompting. The learning curve is steeper than typing a description. Requires understanding Flutter concepts to build anything complex. The distinction between no-code and AI-first builders is worth understanding if you’re deciding between FlutterFlow’s visual approach and the prompt-driven tools on this list. 6. Cursor Best for: Technical founders who want to write their own code with AI assistance Cursor is an AI-enhanced code editor, not an app builder. It’s relevant as a Vibecodeapp alternative only for founders who have some coding ability and want more control than any prompt-to-app tool provides. Think of it as VS Code with deeply integrated AI. You write Swift, React Native, or whatever framework you choose. The AI suggests completions, refactors code, answers questions, and can generate entire functions from descriptions. But you’re driving. Pricing: Free tier available Pro: ~$20/mo (includes ~225 Sonnet requests, ~550 Gemini requests, or ~500 GPT 5 requests) Key strengths: Maximum control over architecture, design patterns, and code quality Works with any programming language or framework Cheapest paid option on this list No vendor lock-in since you’re writing standard code Tradeoffs: You need to understand code. No guided workflow, no screen mapping, no launch assets. Building a full app from scratch takes significantly longer than using a purpose-built app studio. No App Store submission assistance, screenshot generation, or ASO tooling. For a detailed breakdown of when an AI code editor makes sense versus a dedicated app studio, there’s a comparison of x1 and Cursor that covers the tradeoffs. 7. Claude Code Best for: Experienced developers who want maximum flexibility with zero hand-holding Claude Code is Anthropic’s agentic coding tool that runs in the terminal. It can generate entire Swift projects from prompts, scaffold React Native apps, and handle complex refactoring. But it’s a raw tool, not a product. You need your own development environment, Xcode installed, and enough experience to evaluate and fix what it generates. Interestingly, Vibecodeapp itself was powered by Claude Code under the hood. Using Claude Code directly cuts out the middleman but also removes the UI, workflow, and guardrails. Pricing: Pay-per-token (API usage) Costs vary based on model and usage volume Key strengths: Most flexible option on this list No monthly subscription ceiling, you pay for what you use Can tackle problems no app builder handles (custom backends, complex algorithms, niche frameworks) Tradeoffs: No visual design. No launch workflow. No screenshot generation. Pure code output. Requires a working Xcode setup and developer experience. Security research published in January 2026 found that AI-generated applications frequently contain basic logic errors and security vulnerabilities. Three test apps built from the same prompt all exhibited flaws. Without the expertise to audit the output, Claude Code can introduce problems you won’t catch. 8. Vibra Code Best for: Developers who want full control through an open-source, self-hosted solution Vibra Code is the open-source answer to commercial Vibecodeapp alternatives. Built with Claude Code, Expo, React Native, and Convex, it lets you describe what you want, the AI builds it, and you preview on your phone. The entire stack is self-hosted. Pricing: Free, forever. Self-hosted. Key strengths: No vendor lock-in whatsoever Full visibility into how the AI generates code Community-driven development No credit limits or subscription costs Tradeoffs: Requires significant technical setup. This is not a tool for non-technical founders. No managed service means you handle infrastructure, updates, and debugging yourself. Community-supported, not commercially supported. If something breaks at 2 AM before your launch, you’re on your own. Smaller community than commercial tools means fewer templates, examples, and troubleshooting resources. How to Choose the Right Vibecodeapp Alternative The number of options can feel overwhelming, so here’s a simple decision tree. Building for iOS only? x1 (if you want the full guided workflow and launch assets) or Superapp (if budget is the primary constraint). Both produce native Swift output. Need iOS and Android from one tool? Rork (if you want a free tier to test) or Newly (if clean code ownership matters most). Have a technical team that prefers visual building? FlutterFlow gives you Flutter code export and cross-platform compilation. Comfortable writing code yourself? Cursor for AI-assisted coding, Claude Code for terminal-based generation. Want everything free and open source? Vibra Code, but only if you can handle the self-hosting. Don’t forget hidden costs that apply regardless of which tool you pick. Apple’s Developer Program is $99/year. Credit overages on AI tools are common. And the traditional cost of building a mobile app ranges from $40,000 to $400,000+, so even the most expensive option here is a fraction of hiring a development team. For a structured framework to evaluate these tools against your specific needs, the app builder selection checklist walks through every dimension worth considering. What Apple’s Guideline 2.5.2 Means for Your Choice This is the single most important evaluation dimension for anyone building iOS apps in 2026, and it’s the one most competitor listicles ignore. Apple’s Guideline 2.5.2 requires apps to be “self-contained.” They cannot download, install, or execute code that introduces new features or functionality. Vibecodeapp, Replit, and Anything all violated this by acting as “app builders within apps,” essentially running as platforms that generate and execute other apps on the user’s device. Here’s the critical distinction: Apple does not have a specific rule banning vibe-coded apps. If your vibe-coded app runs as a standalone native application and passes all standard review checks, Apple will approve it. The problem is with the builder tool itself running on iOS, not with the apps it produces. Tools that generate code you compile and submit yourself (x1, Superapp, Cursor, Claude Code) are structurally unaffected by 2.5.2. Tools that run generated apps inside a mobile app shell are the ones Apple targeted. Before submitting anything, run through a proper App Store review checklist to catch issues before Apple does. A Note on Security The vibe coding space has a security problem that deserves honest acknowledgment regardless of which tool you choose. Research published in January 2026 found that applications built using AI agents commonly contain basic logic errors and security vulnerabilities. Across three test apps built from the same prompt, all exhibited flaws. One developer on Dev.to described vibe coding as a “frustrating experience” that left them feeling less productive. The emerging consensus in developer communities: you can vibe your way to decent prototypes for apps where quality and security are non-critical. But don’t deploy to production without serious scrutiny, human review, and testing. This applies to every tool on this list. The $4.7 billion vibe coding market is powerful, but it’s not yet a replacement for careful engineering on apps that handle user data or payments. Start building with x1 and test whether the guided studio workflow addresses these quality concerns for your use case. FAQ Is Vibecodeapp still available? Vibecodeapp’s iOS app was blocked from App Store updates in March 2026 under Apple’s Guideline 2.5.2. The web platform may still function, but the core iOS app building and testing workflow was disrupted. Given the Apple crackdown and negative user sentiment on Trustpilot, most founders looking for Vibecodeapp alternatives are better served by tools with clearer App Store compliance. What’s the cheapest Vibecodeapp alternative? Vibra Code is completely free since it’s open source and self-hosted, but it requires technical skill to set up. Among managed tools, Rork, Superapp, and Newly all start at $25/month. Cursor starts at roughly $20/month but requires coding knowledge. For true native iOS output at the lowest price, Superapp at $25/month is hard to beat. Can I build an iOS app without a Mac? Yes. Superapp runs entirely in the browser and builds in the cloud, so you can develop native Swift apps from Windows or Linux. Newly also supports iOS builds from Windows. Cloud-based tools are eliminating the Mac requirement, though you may still want a Mac for final testing before App Store submission. Do I need coding experience to use these tools? Not for most of them. x1, Rork, Superapp, and Newly are all designed for non-technical founders. You describe what you want in plain English, and the AI generates the app. FlutterFlow has a visual builder that requires understanding app logic but not writing code. Cursor and Claude Code are explicitly for people who code. For a deeper guide, see this overview of the best app builders for non-technical founders . Will Apple reject my AI-built app? Not because it was built with AI. Apple rejects apps that violate specific guidelines, not apps built with specific tools. If your AI-built app is a standalone native binary that passes all standard review checks (proper metadata, no private API usage, correct permissions, reasonable functionality), Apple will approve it. The March 2026 crackdown targeted the builder tools themselves, not the apps they produced. How much should I actually budget for an AI-built app? Take the monthly subscription cost and roughly double it to account for credit overages from bug-fixing iterations. Add Apple’s $99/year Developer Program fee. For a realistic total, expect $500 to $2,000 to go from idea to published App Store app using any tool on this list. That’s still a fraction of the $40,000 to $400,000+ traditional development costs. What’s the difference between native Swift and React Native output? Native Swift apps are written in Apple’s own programming language and compiled directly for iOS. React Native apps are written in JavaScript and compiled to native components through a bridge layer. Both produce real App Store apps, but native Swift typically offers better performance, smoother animations, and easier access to the latest iOS features. React Native’s advantage is cross-platform: one codebase for both iOS and Android.

body_text: Lyft Reports Strong Q2 2026 Results August 06, 2026 4:05pm EDT Related Documents Earnings Webcast Audio Supplemental Slides PDF Prepared Remarks PDF Record Active Riders of over 30 million globally Growth accelerated in Q2 delivering record Rides and Gross Bookings SAN FRANCISCO--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Lyft, Inc. (Nasdaq: LYFT) today announced financial results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026. “We have surpassed 30 million Active Riders globally, our highest ever, as more people embed Lyft into their everyday lives,” said Lyft CEO David Risher. “This milestone is driven by our customer obsession and operational excellence, and fuels our transformation into a hybrid transportation platform while we deliver strong financial performance. So buckle up, the opportunity ahead is massive, and we’re just getting started.” “The business delivered acceleration in the second quarter, with growth in Rides and Gross Bookings reaching record levels, alongside continued strong cash generation of over $1 billion for the trailing twelve months,” said CFO Erin Brewer. “These results reflect the strength of our foundation and give us confidence in the road ahead.” Second Quarter 2026 Financial Highlights Gross Bookings of $5.5 billion, up 23% year over year. Revenue of $1.8 billion, up 16% year over year. Net income was up 25% year over year to $50.3 million compared to $40.3 million in Q2'25. Net income as a percentage of Gross Bookings of 0.9%, flat compared to Q2'25. Adjusted EBITDA up 37% year over year to $177.2 million compared to $129.4 million in Q2'25. Adjusted EBITDA margin as a percentage of Gross Bookings of 3.2% compared to 2.9% in Q2'25. Net cash provided by operating activities of $349.9 million compared to $343.7 million in Q2'25. For the trailing twelve months, net cash provided by operating activities was $1.2 billion. Free cash flow of $319.6 million compared to $329.4 million in Q2'25. For the trailing twelve months, free cash flow was $1.1 billion. Second Quarter 2026 Operational Highlights Record Active Riders, our leading indicator of growth, was up 17% year over year to 30.5 million, the 7th consecutive quarter of double-digit growth. Rides accelerated sequentially to record levels, up 12% year over year to 262 million, with global strength across Freenow by Lyft in Europe, North American rideshare, and Lyft Urban Solutions. Approximately 30% of North American rideshare rides were linked to a partnership, an all-time high as we continue to be a good partner and collaborate to create value for our riders and partners. In Nashville, in partnership with Waymo, our fleet operations officially began in June and are running smoothly as we gear up for the opening of our 80,000-square-foot purpose-built AV depot in October. Lyft and Curb expanded their strategic partnership to New York City, the largest taxi market in the U.S., reflecting our strategy of expanding transport options for riders through partnerships with established, licensed operators. Third Quarter 2026 Outlook Gross Bookings of approximately $5.50 billion to $5.67 billion, up approximately 15% to 19% year over year. Adjusted EBITDA of approximately $183 million to $203 million Adjusted EBITDA margin (calculated as a percentage of Gross Bookings) of approximately 3.3% to 3.6%. We have not provided the forward-looking GAAP equivalent to our non-GAAP outlook or a GAAP reconciliation as a result of the uncertainty regarding, and the potential variability of reconciling items which include, but are not limited to, stock-based compensation, income tax, legal, tax, and regulatory reserve changes and settlements, and costs related to acquisitions. Accordingly, a reconciliation of these non-GAAP guidance metrics to their corresponding GAAP equivalent is not available without unreasonable effort. However, it is important to note that the reconciling items could have a significant effect on future GAAP results. We have provided historical reconciliations of GAAP to non-GAAP metrics in tables at the end of this release. For more information regarding the non-GAAP financial measures discussed in this earnings release, please see “GAAP to non-GAAP Reconciliations” below. Financial and Operational Results Three Months Ended June 30, 2026 March 31, 2026 June 30, 2025 (in millions, except for percentages) Active Riders 30.5 28.3 26.1 Rides 262.4 236.9 234.8 Gross Bookings $ 5,504.2 $ 4,946.0 $ 4,490.1 Revenue $ 1,843.5 $ 1,650.5 $ 1,588.2 Net income $ 50.3 $ 14.2 $ 40.3 Net income as a percentage of Gross Bookings 0.9 % 0.3 % 0.9 % Adjusted EBITDA $ 177.2 $ 132.8 $ 129.4 Adjusted EBITDA margin (calculated as a percentage of Gross Bookings) 3.2 % 2.7 % 2.9 % Net cash provided by operating activities $ 349.9 $ 307.7 $ 343.7 Free cash flow $ 319.6 $ 287.3 $ 329.4 Note: Information on our key metrics and non-GAAP financial measures is also available on our Investor Relations page. Definitions of Key Metrics Active Riders The number of Active Riders is a key indicator of the scale of Lyft’s user community. Lyft defines Active Riders as all unique riders who have taken at least one ride during the quarter. If a ride is requested by another organization or person for the benefit of a rider, that rider is only included in the calculation of Active Riders if the ride is accessible in the rider’s Lyft App. Rides Rides represent the level of usage of our multimodal platform. Lyft defines Rides as the total number of rides completed on our multimodal platform that contribute to our revenue. These include any Rides taken through our Lyft App. If multiple riders take a private rideshare ride, including situations where one party picks up another party on the way to a destination, or splits the bill, we count this as a single rideshare ride. Each unique segment of a Shared Ride is considered a single Ride. For example, if two riders successfully match in Shared Ride mode and both complete their Rides, we count this as two Rides. We have largely shifted away from Shared Rides, and now only offer Shared Rides in limited markets. Lyft includes all Rides taken by riders via our Concierge offering, even though such riders may be excluded from the definition of Active Riders unless the ride is accessible in that rider’s Lyft App. Gross Bookings Gross Bookings is a key indicator of the scale and impact of our overall platform. Lyft defines Gross Bookings as the total dollar value of transactions including any applicable taxes, tolls and fees, for rides and other offerings provided by Lyft, excluding tips to drivers. Adjusted EBITDA margin (calculated as a percentage of Gross Bookings) Adjusted EBITDA margin (calculated as a percentage of Gross Bookings) is calculated by dividing Adjusted EBITDA for a period by Gross Bookings for the same period. For the definition of Adjusted EBITDA, refer to “Non-GAAP Financial Measures”. Non-GAAP Financial Measures To supplement Lyft's financial information presented in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles in the United States of America, or GAAP, Lyft considers certain financial measures that are not prepared in accordance with GAAP, including Adjusted EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA margin (calculated as a percentage of Gross Bookings) and free cash flow. Lyft defines Adjusted EBITDA as net income (loss) adjusted for interest expense, other income (expense), net, provision for (benefit from) income taxes, depreciation and amortization, stock-based compensation expense, payroll tax expense related to stock-based compensation, as well as, if applicable, sublease income, gain from lease termination, restructuring charges, costs related to acquisitions, divestitures and other corporate matters, and certain legal, tax, and regulatory reserve changes and settlements. Adjusted EBITDA margin (calculated as a percentage of Gross Bookings) is calculated by dividing Adjusted EBITDA for a period by Gross Bookings for the same period and is considered a key metric. Lyft defines free cash flow as GAAP net cash provided by (used in) operating activities less purchases of property and equipment and scooter fleet. Lyft subleases certain office space and earns sublease income. Sublease income is included within other income, net on the condensed consolidated statement of operations, while the related lease expense is included within operating expenses and loss from operations. Lyft believes the adjustment to include sublease income in Adjusted EBITDA is useful to investors by enabling them to better assess Lyft’s operating performance, including the benefits of recent transactions, by presenting sublease income as a contra-expense to the related lease charges that are part of operating expenses. Lyft excludes certain costs related to acquisitions including due diligence costs, professional fees in connection with an acquisition, certain financing costs, and certain integration-related expenses. We believe excluding costs related to acquisitions, divestitures and other corporate matters facilitates the comparison of our financial results to our historical operating results and to other companies in the industry. Certain legal, tax, and regulatory reserve changes and settlements are primarily related to certain reserves and/or settlements for significant legal proceedings or governmental investigations and the associated fees. These matters have limited precedent, cover extended historical periods and are unpredictable in both magnitude and timing, therefore are distinct from normal, recurring legal, tax and regulatory matters and related expenses incurred in our ongoing operating performance. We believe free cash flow is a useful indicator of liquidity that provides our management with information about our ability to generate or use cash to enhance the strength of our balance sheet, further invest in our business and pursue potential strategic initiatives. Free cash flow has certain limitations, including that it does not reflect our future contractual commitments and it does not represent the total increase or decrease in our cash balance for a given period. Free cash flow does not necessarily represent funds available for discretionary use and is not necessarily a measure of our ability to fund our cash needs.
